stem:
Fig. 8.1 shows a circuit that produces rectification of an alternating input voltage.

[[fig:f1]]

The input voltage *V*₍IN₎ is sinusoidal. The rectified output voltage *V*₍OUT₎ is applied across resistor R.

The variation of *V*₍IN₎ with time *t* has amplitude *V*₀ and period *T*, as shown in Fig. 8.2.

[[fig:f2]]

The root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of *V*₍IN₎ is 6.0 V.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: State the type of rectification produced by the circuit of Fig. 8.1.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.lead:
Resistor R has resistance 45 Ω.

Assume that there is no p.d. across the diode when it is conducting.
parts.text: Determine the peak power *P*₀ in the resistor.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
On Fig. 8.3, sketch the variation of the power *P* in the resistor with *t* between *t* = 0 and *t* = 2*T*.

[[fig:f3]]

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Use the answer in (b)(ii) to explain why the mean power in the resistor is ¼ *P*₀.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Use the information in (b)(ii) to determine the r.m.s. value of *V*₍OUT₎.

figures.caption: Fig. 8.1
figures.alt: A circuit with an input voltage across the left-hand terminals, a diode in the top wire and a resistor R across which the output voltage is measured.

figures.caption: Fig. 8.2
figures.alt: A graph of the sinusoidal input voltage against time, showing amplitude V₀ and a period T.

figures.caption: Fig. 8.3
figures.alt: A blank gridded graph for power against time, with the vertical axis marked at zero, half P₀ and P₀, and the horizontal axis marked from zero to 2T.
